To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in 65% of glioma patients with long-term seizure freedom a shared decision was taken to discontinue AEDs, but seizure recurrence was observed in 26% of these patients, of whom 58% had tumor progression.
in 65% of glioma patients with seizure freedom, AED withdrawal was considered and in 26% AED withdrawal was followed by seizure recurrence.

in 65% of glioma patients with long-term seizure freedom, a shared decision was reached to discontinue antiepileptic drug treatment, and that 26% of these patients had seizure recurrence during a median follow-up period of 2.3 years (range 0.5-5.3 years).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the decision-making process in glioma patients who have been seizure free for at least two years, and whether or not to withdraw antiepileptic drug (AED) treatment.
the question of when and whether anticonvulsant drugs should be withdrawn in patients with a low grade or anaplatic glioma after long term seizure freedom.
the decision-making process and the outcome after AED withdrawal in patients with low-grade and anaplastic glial tumors who have been seizure-free for at least 1 year.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AEDs should only be withdrawn in patients with a low risk of tumor recurrence and in those who have been seizure-free for at least 1 year.
the evidence is not yet sufficient to make a clear recommendation for or against the withdrawal of AEDs in patients with low-grade or anaplastic astrocytoma with long-term seizure freedom.
in patients with low-grade glioma and long-term seizure freedom, AEDs can be discontinued in carefully selected patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decision on whether to continue or withdraw AEDs should be based on an individualized shared-decision making process, and should be made in collaboration with a neuro-oncologist.
the decision to withdraw AED should be made by a multidisciplinary team and only in selected patients.
patients who have had long-term seizure freedom after treatment for a glioma should have a shared decision with their treating neuro-oncologist to consider whether to stop their AEDs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

AED withdrawal is a shared decision between the neuro-oncologists and the patients, and that AED withdrawal should be considered in carefully-selected patients with a presumed lower risk of tumor progression.
AED withdrawal is not a standard of care in glioma patients with long-term seizure freedom.

shared decision-making is feasible and that AED withdrawal can be considered in carefully-selected patients with low-grade glioma and anaplastic oligodendroglioma who have been seizure-free for at least 1 year.
